SOURCE 1 (Public Sénat) :
En continuant d’affirmer qu’Eric Zemmour a sa place dans une primaire de la droite, David Lisnard met à mal le camp de Gabriel Attal, pour qui une primaire avec le candidat Reconquête « n’est pas possible ». Avec Eric Zemmour, « vous flinguez la primaire », pointe Bruno Retailleau. L’intéressé dément tout calcul qui lui permettrait de tuer la primaire, sans le dire. « C’est un commentaire malveillant », répond à publicsenat.fr David Lisnard, qui prône une « grande primaire ouverte », où la présence d’Edouard Philippe serait indispensable. Mais il prévient : si la primaire ne se fait pas, il ira jusqu’au bout.
Présomption de légitime défense pour les forces de l’ordre : le Sénat se divise sur cette proposition de loi polémique
Adoptée à l’Assemblée nationale en juillet dernier, avec l’appui des députés du socle gouvernemental et de l’alliance Rassemblement national-Union des droites pour la République, la proposition de loi visant à instaurer une présomption de légitime défense sera examinée au Sénat en fin de journée.
« Il faut arrêter de laisser penser que ce texte aura un effet désinhibant pour les forces de l’ordre »
Le texte déposé par le député Les Républicains Éric Pauget, qui prévoyait initialement une présomption de légitime défense des forces de l’ordre, a été réécrit par le gouvernement devant l’Assemblée. Contrairement à ce que laisse penser son intitulé, le texte ne vient pas ajouter un nouveau cas d’usage des armes des forces de l’ordre tel que prévu à l’article L. 435-1 du code de la sécurité intérieure, ni modifier le régime juridique de la légitime défense, prévu par le code pénal, mais instaure une présomption « simple » de respect du cadre légal d’usage des armes. Lorsqu’ils font usage de leurs armes, policiers et gendarmes « sont présumés avoir agi » dans le cadre de la loi. Il procède ainsi à une inversion de la charge de la preuve, qui viendra apporter une protection juridique supplémentaire aux policiers et aux gendarmes, selon les défenseurs du texte.
« Ce n’est pas la mort du petit cheval. Il faut arrêter de laisser penser que ce texte aura un effet désinhibant pour les forces de l’ordre. L’usage des armes reste dans le même cadre légal, les cas d’usage définis par la loi de 2017 de Bernard Cazeneuve. En revanche, depuis dix ans, le nombre d’agressions envers les forces de l’ordre a explosé. On assume ce message de soutien aux forces de l’ordre qui en ont besoin en ce moment avec toutes ces problématiques liées au maintien de l’ordre », indique Lauriane Josende, la rapporteure LR du texte.
Le contexte politique et social va en effet jouer un rôle important dans le déroulé des débats. L’examen de ce texte intervient à l’heure où les policiers se mobilisent pour obtenir une revalorisation de leur prime de risque après des semaines de contestation lycéenne et sociale et à quelques jours des élections professionnelles dans la fonction publique. Une délégation du syndicat Alliance a d’ailleurs été reçue mercredi par le ministre de l’Intérieur Laurent Nuñez.
À l’approche de l’élection présidentielle, le gouvernement et la droite sont accusés par la gauche de courir après l’extrême droite. L’exécutif avait d’ailleurs décidé de couper l’herbe sous le pied du nouveau groupe RN-UDR du Sénat en inscrivant le texte dans son temps réservé, alors que le groupe présidé par Edwige Diaz l’avait pourtant inscrit dans sa niche parlementaire prévue le 10 décembre.
« Le procès des policiers qui ont tabassé Michel Zecler devrait tous nous éclairer »
La majorité sénatoriale de droite souhaite un vote conforme pour une application rapide du texte et n’a pas modifié la proposition de loi en commission ni déposé d’amendements en séance. Les écologistes, socialistes et communistes du Sénat ont, quant à eux, déposé trois motions de rejet et une quarantaine d’amendements. A minima, les socialistes souhaitent exclure l’application de la présomption d’usage légal lorsque l’usage de l’arme a entraîné la mort.
« Le procès des policiers qui ont tabassé Michel Zecler devrait tous nous éclairer. Entre le moment où un fait est commis et le moment où sort la version officielle de la police, qui, par principe, n’est pas mise en doute, il y a eu une concertation entre les témoins et même une rédaction de faux PV. L’intérêt du régime actuel est de permettre les saisies et le placement en garde à vue, qui permet l’absence de concertation entre les mises en cause. Il faut au moins conserver le régime actuel lorsque les tirs ont entraîné la mort d’une personne qui, par définition, ne sera plus là pour donner sa version », appuie la sénatrice PS Marie-Pierre de La Gontrie. L’élue de Paris rappelle que ce texte répond à « une demande très ancienne des policiers ». « Aujourd’hui on a un gouvernement faible et un ministre de l’Intérieur qui cède », déplore-t-elle.
Sauf surprise, le texte devrait être adopté, même si certains sénateurs centristes et macronistes pourraient voter contre ou s’abstenir. « Cela envoie un très mauvais message alors que les lycéens et les étudiants manifestent avec des revendications importantes. Ce texte ne servira à rien, à part faire monter Marine Le Pen dans les sondages », a déclaré à l’AFP la sénatrice centriste Olivia Richard.
« Le contexte lycéen sert de prétexte à certains pour se donner bonne conscience, alors que ça n’a rien à voir, puisque ce texte ne porte pas sur l’usage des armes intermédiaires. Juridiquement le maintien de l’ordre est régi par d’autres dispositions », insiste Lauriane Josende.
La mobilisation se déroulera aussi hors de l’hémicycle. Plusieurs organisations de défense des droits humains ont appelé à manifester devant le Sénat à 15 h pour s’opposer à cette proposition de loi.

SOURCE 2 (RMC) :
Le Sénat examine, ce jeudi 19 novembre, une proposition de loi, qui vise à "reconnaître une présomption de légitime défense aux forces de l'ordre". Concrètement, ce court texte d'un article permet de donner aux policiers et gendarmes, lorsqu'ils utilisent leur arme à feu, une présomption de légitime défense.
Déjà adopté en juillet à l'Assemblée, le texte pourrait donc être définitivement adopté ce jeudi soir s'il est voté dans les mêmes termes au Sénat. Plusieurs syndicats et associations se sont opposés au texte (CGT, CFDT, Solidaires, Unef, LDH, SAF, FSU, Syndicat de la Magistrature, etc.).
L'opposition de gauche s'inquiète
Au Sénat, les groupes de gauche sont très remontés contre ce texte. Pour la présidente du groupe écologiste Mélanie Vogel, ce texte crée un permis de tuer pour les forces de l'ordre: "L'objet du texte est de permettre de présumer que lorsque des policiers tirent, ils agissent légalement, même lorsqu'ils ne sont pas attaqués."
"C'est une rupture du pacte républicain qui est vertigineuse. Non seulement, il y aura plus de morts, mais en plus, ces morts ne seront pas jugés comme il se doit", craint Mélanie Vogel.
Au contraire, c'est une accusation infondée selon les défenseurs du texte. "Il ne s'agit pas du tout d'un permis de tuer", assure la sénatrice LR Lauriane Josende. Elle estime que cette mesure est essentielle pour aider les forces de l'ordre. Les agents qui utilisent leur arme et touchent une personne se retrouvent systématiquement en garde à vue. Ils hésitent donc parfois dans des situations d'urgence.
"C'est jamais une partie de plaisir d'utiliser son arme, donc c'est vrai que de leur dire 'écoutez on présume que les conditions sont remplies et à charge de l'enquête de démontrer que c'est le contraire', c'est quand même leur témoigner une confiance dont ils ont besoin aujourd'hui", défend la sénatrice LR.
Lauriane Josende ajoute qu'une enquête aura toujours lieu. Mais cela ne suffit pas à convaincre les groupes de gauche, qui ont déjà annoncé saisir le Conseil constitutionnel en cas d'adoption du texte.

The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
The United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has held a state responsible for the crime.
Judges of the International Court of Justice voted 9-6 that the military's 2017 crackdown was carried out with intent to destroy the long-persecuted Muslim minority. Myanmar's military-backed government has not yet responded to the ruling at the time of writing.
Brought by Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, according to a legal expert.
But for Ma Roga Bibi, a Rohingya who fled Maungdaw township in northern Rakhine state, the impact was immediate.
"I feel wonderful and grateful," said the 18-year-old, who lives in the world's largest refugee settlement in Bangladesh. "It was an emotional, historic day."
Genocidal campaign
For several weeks in August and September 2017, the Myanmar military attacked and burned to the ground hundreds of Rohingya villages. Soldiers committed rapes and massacred women, men as well as children.
The court estimated that about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. It cited estimates that up to 2,109 Rohingya children younger than 5 died, and found the violence was systematic, including the burning of all or parts of 392 villages.
Ma Roga Bibi, then age 9, was one of about 700,000 people to flee to Bangladesh, joining earlier refugee waves. The camps sprawl across a narrow coastal strip a few miles from Cox's Bazar, a busy beach town near Myanmar. Rohingya are denied citizenship on both sides of the border.
"Recognition alone is not enough," she said. "We need justice, accountability, and the opportunity to return home with dignity."
She wants to be a doctor, adding, "in our Rohingya community, there is no girl doctor."
Khin Khin Myint, 18, a refugee leader in activist group Rohingya Youth Voice from Buthidaung Township, also in Camp 16, said Rohingya women and girls have experienced "unimaginable suffering."
"We want the world to listen to survivors, recognize their courage, and include women in decisions about our future," she said. "We expect the international community to move beyond a statement of sympathy."
Rejected defense
Myanmar had argued its military was conducting counterinsurgency operations against an armed group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The court said the military failed to distinguish between civilians and alleged insurgents, and that the scale and nature of the violence could not be explained by counterterrorism.
"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," said ICJ president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa.
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, a human rights group based in Geneva, said the court found evidence from the U.N. and rights organizations credible, and that counterterrorism operations were not a defense to Myanmar's argument.
She said the ruling will affect future genocide cases, including South Africa's case against Israel, on questions such as genocidal intent and state responsibility.
"Although every case must ultimately be decided on its own evidence," she said.
The judgment is binding on Myanmar and on all states that have ratified the Genocide Convention, she explained. All countries should review trade agreements, including arms and jet fuel supplies, and financial and economic ties with the junta, she said, while supporting accountability and reparations for the Rohingya. But the court, which hears disputes between states, can't enforce its decisions.
A group long denied recognition
In Myanmar, Rohingya are widely regarded as interlopers from Bangladesh, despite generations of roots in Myanmar.
Iwasawa, however, identified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group, saying their language and art set them apart, and that they self-identify as such. He said they have been discriminated against by Myanmar "for decades" and qualify as a protected group.
The United States had previously reached a similar conclusion. In 2022, the Biden administration formally determined that Myanmar's military had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya during its 2016 and 2017 operations.
But tensions have mounted between the Trump administration and international justice bodies. In a statement to NPR on Thursday, the State Department expressed support for Rohingya refugees but raised doubts about the International Court of Justice. "The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ. We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," the State Department said.
In October, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz wrote online, "The ICJ must not be allowed to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide" so it can later be weaponized against U.S. and allied soldiers.
Yet international human rights organizations and the United Nations applauded the court's judgment.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres called it "a powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and said it reaffirms that "impunity for such horrific acts must not stand."
The judgment does not order Myanmar to grant citizenship, saying such the issue fell outside the scope of the measures being considered to prevent future atrocities.
However, Myanmar must take steps to investigate people suspected of involvement in the crimes and prosecute them if warranted, said the court. It also found Myanmar must provide restitution and compensation, with the amount to be set in future proceedings.
The order to enable displaced Rohingya to return runs into a hard reality: The territory is now controlled by ethnic Rakhine armed group the Arakan Army.
Rakhine state has been ravaged by conflict between the military and the group, which now controls most of it.
Su Mon, a senior analyst at the independent conflict monitor Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, said the Rohingya in Myanmar and in the camps are "threatened by multiple armed groups," including Rohingya armed groups, the Arakan Army and the military.
Nearly all are stateless, she said, with few viable ways to earn a living or get food. Many are "on the verge of acute famine" because of aid shortfalls in the camps and a junta blockade in Rakhine.
"Unless the broader conflict dynamics in Rakhine state improve or credible guarantees of safety are secured from all armed actors, the prospects for displaced Rohingya to return to their homes remain bleak," she added.
She urged the military to halt airstrikes, drone attacks and the use of advanced weaponry in northern Rakhine, lift its blockade and give humanitarian groups full access, including in Arakan Army-controlled areas.
Lorcán Lovett reported from Thailand. Michele Kelemen contributed reporting from Washington, D.C.

With vote counts concluding and the closest House races being decided, we now have a clearer picture of Democrats' dominant midterms.
Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That's a 14-point spread on the House ballot.

ABSTRACT
Impact measurement is central to impact investing and social entrepreneurship, yet little is known 
about whether firms benefit privately from measuring impact. We conduct the first randomized 
controlled trial of an impact measurement intervention among high-growth social enterprises in 
India. Treated firms exhibit nearly twice as much revenue growth and raise nearly twice as much 
capital as control firms. In a companion experiment with early-stage investors, we find that 
investors respond strongly to quantified impact metrics but not to generic qualitative impact 
statements. Together, our results show that impact measurement can shape firm growth and 
capital allocation.

MEASURING THE IMPACT OF IMPACT MEASUREMENT 1
I. Introduction
The last two decades have seen tremendous growth in the scale and legitimacy of the movement
to combine social impact with corporate interests. Leading estimates suggest that impact investors
control more than one and a half trillion dollars in assets under management (Hand et al., 2024),
and that social enterprises generate more than two trillion dollars in annual revenue worldwide
(World Economic Forum and Schwab Foundation for Social Entrepreneurship, 2024). Impact
investing rests on the premise that capital should be allocated not only to profitable firms, but
also to firms that create social value. Yet this premise creates a measurement problem (Serafeim
and Trinh, 2020). Profits are measured because accounting, taxation, and investor reporting make
financial measurement unavoidable. Social impact, by contrast, is often costly to quantify, difficult
to compare across firms, and communicated through qualitative narratives. This raises a basic
economic question: are there private returns to measuring social returns?
We answer this question with two experiments. In the first, we randomize hands-on support
that helps Indian social enterprises collect stakeholder-level impact data and translate it into a
personalized impact report. Treated firms grow faster and raise more capital. In the second, we
randomize the impact information shown to early-stage investors and show that investors respond
to quantified impact metrics, but not to generic impact narratives.
We conducted the first experiment in partnership with Villgro, India’s largest incubator of
social enterprises. All 163 participating firms—spanning industries such as agribusiness, health,
energy, and education—were offered the same impact measurement and management (IMM) course.
Random assignment determined whether firms also received hands-on implementation support:
treatment firms worked through several one-on-one sessions with Villgro representatives to choose
an IMM framework, define impact indicators, plan stakeholder outreach, and operationalize data
collection; their customers, employees, and suppliers were then surveyed by the research team,
and the results were synthesized in a personalized impact report summarizing stakeholder surplus
measures.1 Control firms received the same course but not the full implementation support or
report until the end of the study.
The intervention had a large impact on both revenue growth and access to capital. Both groups
grew, but treatment firms experienced approximately an additional USD 20,000 in revenue growth,
bringing total treatment-group growth to nearly double that of control firms. Similarly, treatment
group firms raised an additional USD 43,000 in external funding, again a doubling relative to
1By surplus, we mean the value created for a stakeholder beyond the stakeholder’s next-best alternative: for customers,
willingness-to-pay net of price; for workers and suppliers, compensation or payments net of reservation values.
MEASURING THE IMPACT OF IMPACT MEASUREMENT 2
control. Our results are not driven by a small handful of outliers. We see a distributional shift in
both revenue and capital raised, and a statistically significant increase in median revenue growth
and additional capital raised. These findings document private returns to implementing impact
measurement. For social enterprises, faster growth could also expand the reach of products and
services intended to benefit customers and other stakeholders, thus potentially improving social
impact more broadly.
The intervention was designed to mirror how firms typically implement impact measurement,
and therefore combines several complementary components. This bundled design captures the
policy-relevant effect of moving firms from training to implementation, but does not allow us to
separately identify the contribution of each component or the specific mechanisms at work. The
intervention naturally creates two forms of decision-relevant information. Internally, the process
of choosing indicators, engaging stakeholders, and collecting stakeholder-level data may help firms
learn which customers and use cases generate the most value. Externally, quantified impact metrics
may make impact claims more credible to investors.
Access to capital is both a central outcome for early-stage social enterprises and a possible
channel through which impact measurement affects firm growth. We therefore run a companion
experiment that isolates investor demand for quantified impact information. We conducted a field
experiment with 223 early-stage investors with experience investing in Indian startups, inspired by
non-deceptive variations of resume audit studies commonly used in the labor literature (Harrison
and List, 2004; Kessler et al., 2019).2 Investors were recruited through Villgro and Harvard
Business School networks, direct outreach, and a professional survey firm. Investors were shown
hypothetical startup profiles, with characteristics drawn at random from the distribution of startups
participating in our first experiment. Investors then rated these profiles based on their investment
interest. Ratings were incentivized by the offer to introduce investors to real startups seeking
capital, whose characteristics matched the preferences investors expressed through their ratings.
Randomizing firm attributes allows us to infer the causal impact of any firm characteristic on
investor interest, holding other firm characteristics constant.
Our primary comparison of interest is how a startup’s social impact is communicated. Some
profiles reported only baseline customer demographics, such as average monthly customer income
and the share of customers earning less than $5 per day. Others added a qualitative impact
statement, meant to represent the narrative approach to communicating impact adopted by many

(2023).
MEASURING THE IMPACT OF IMPACT MEASUREMENT 3
social enterprises. Finally, others reported customer surplus, one of the key quantitative impact
metrics covered in the IMM course and implemented in the first experiment.
Our main result is that investor interest is strongly responsive to quantified impact metrics.
Moving a startup from below- to above-median customer surplus increases investor interest by
an amount comparable to moving the firm from unprofitable to profitable. By contrast, generic
qualitative impact statements have a small and statistically insignificant effect on investor interest.
Investors therefore do not appear to reward impact language per se; they respond to quantified
evidence of impact.
Our results contribute first to the body of work on impact measurement, impact investing, and
social entrepreneurship (e.g., Serafeim et al., 2019; Allcott et al., 2026b). Most related is the
work establishing a link between social impact and firm performance (e.g., Porter and Kramer,
2011; Edmans, 2011; Eccles et al., 2014; Henderson and Van den Steen, 2015; Khan et al., 2016;
Lins et al., 2017). Our main contribution is to provide causal evidence on the private returns to
implementing impact measurement. To our knowledge, this is the first randomized field experiment
focused on the implementation of impact measurement practices.
Second, we speak to the experimental literature on entrepreneurship training and management
practices (see Karlan and Valdivia (2011) and Bloom et al. (2013) for examples on micro-firms
and large firms, respectively, and McKenzie et al. (2025) for a review). Related to our focus, in the
context of micro-entrepreneurs, Kaul et al. (2025) show that customer feedback seeking can improve
performance and generate spillovers to customers not directly solicited for feedback. Specific to
startups, Camuffo et al. (2020) and Bailey et al. (2026) both find that entrepreneurship training
programs cause startups to more quickly abandon their ideas. We contribute to this literature by
studying the impact of a training program explicitly targeted toward high-growth social enterprises,
and focusing on impact measurement, demonstrating that this type of program can have meaningful
consequences for firm growth and the ability to raise capital.
Finally, we contribute to the experimental literature on investor social preferences. Existing
work asks whether investors value social impact and how they trade it off against financial returns.
For example, Humphrey et al. (2021) identify asymmetries between social benefits and harms, and
Heeb et al. (2023) argue that investors respond to relative, but not absolute, levels of impact. In
contrast, Bonnefon et al. (2025) present evidence that some investors have linear preferences for
impact that are symmetric between harms and benefits. Landier et al. (2026) argue that investors
value corporate intent in addition to realized social benefits, Bonnefon et al. (2025) and Green and
Roth (2025) characterize the degree to which investors have consequentialist social preferences,
MEASURING THE IMPACT OF IMPACT MEASUREMENT 4
and Allcott et al. (2026a) show that investor responses to sustainability disclosures depend in part
on how intuitively the information is presented. We study the information problem behind those
preferences: when impact is communicated in different ways, what type of evidence moves investor
demand? Our results show that investors respond more strongly to quantified impact metrics than
to generic qualitative impact narratives. Thus, the form of impact measurement matters for the
allocation of impact capital.
II. Experiment #1: The Impact of Impact Measurement
Our main experiment was conducted in partnership with Villgro—India’s largest incubator of
social enterprises. Representatives from Villgro, together with faculty from Harvard Business
School and the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, offered all 163 participating firms
the same impact measurement and management (IMM) course. The course was common to both
experimental arms, holding fixed exposure to IMM concepts, language, and certification. Random
assignment determined whether firms also received the remaining components of a practical IMM
implementation engagement: one-on-one support to select a framework, define indicators, and plan
stakeholder outreach; stakeholder surveys conducted by the research team; and synthesis of the
results in a personalized impact report. The treatment therefore isolates the incremental effect of
moving from IMM training to implementation, rather than the effect of classroom exposure alone.
A. Impact Measurement and Management Course
Startup participants were recruited through Villgro’s network. Active startups that had partici-
pated in previous Villgro programs, attended Villgro events, or otherwise indicated a desire to be
notified of Villgro programming were directly contacted to participate in the course. Represen-
tatives from Villgro also circulated several announcements of the course through its social media
accounts. All startups with a social impact focus were invited to apply to the program.
In total, 163 eligible startups (out of 277 complete applications) participated in the program.3
The two primary selection criteria were that the startup conveyed plausible ambitions to achieve

The program was designed to build small and growing businesses’ capacity to measure and monitor
their impact, and participation was not limited to firms already incubated by Villgro. Our sample
spans the sectors and stages described below, but reflects self-selection into an IMM program; the
results are most directly relevant to growth-oriented social enterprises interested in improving these

The course ran in seven two-hour Zoom sessions every other week from April to June 2023—see
Appendix Figure A1 for the intervention and data-collection timeline and Appendix Section C for
the course overview.4 The course covered three main components that largely followed the content of
the Harvard Business School elective course “Data for Impact.” First, participants learned to outline
their theory of change, the mapping from their core business activities and outputs to societal or
environmental impact, and to make explicit the assumptions required for their business activities to
have their intended impact. Second, participants were introduced to three approaches to measuring
social or environmental impact. The Global Impact Investing Network’s (GIIN) Impact Reporting
and Investment Standards (IRIS+) framework provides standardized, sector-specific KPIs linked to
existing empirical evidence. Acumen’s Lean Data approach uses short customer surveys to capture
how products affect users’ lives. Finally, an economic approach based on customer, employee,
and supplier surplus uses willingness-to-pay, compensation, reservation values, and transaction
data to quantify value created for different stakeholders.5 Together, these approaches emphasize
direct stakeholder data and quantitative evaluation as the gold standard for impact measurement.
Third, the course covered tactics for communicating social and environmental impact to employees,
donors, and investors.
B. Intervention
Beginning in April 2023, treatment firms received hands-on support to operationalize impact
measurement. The treatment was designed to approximate a practical IMM engagement, in which
classroom concepts are translated into firm-specific metrics, stakeholder surveys, data collection,
and reporting. Each treated firm was assigned a junior Villgro representative and typically met

Abstract
Background
Serum or plasma concentrations of creatinine and urea are the usual laboratory parameters measured to assess acute kidney injury (AKI) in patients with suspected severe malaria. Creatinine is preferred for estimation of the glomerular filtration rate, but the current threshold for defining severe malaria (>265 μmol/L or a urea >20 mmol/L) is based on adult values and does not reflect the large difference between children and adults in normal values resulting from differences in muscle mass. We reevaluated these thresholds and their prognostic significance in severe malaria using individual patient data from large prospective studies.
Methods and findings
We pooled individual patient data from 22,663 patients recruited into 14 studies of severe malaria of whom 16,441 were included in the primary analysis population. Patients were included in the primary analysis population if their age (if missing, imputed from weight or height), coma status on admission, and either an admission serum or plasma creatinine or urea measurement (blood urea nitrogen, BUN), were all recorded. The primary outcome was mortality by day 28. The secondary outcome was the admission plasma Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein 2 (PfHRP2) concentration (a measure of parasite biomass). Bayesian penalised spline regression models were used to characterise the age-specific relationships (interaction with age) between the outcome and the absolute creatinine, the creatinine fold change relative to the age/weight predicted baseline, and the absolute urea. The models adjusted for coma status and calendar year, with nested random additive effects by study site and study. We estimated threshold plasma or serum creatinine and urea concentrations associated with >5% mortality with probability > 0.9. The majority (84%; 13,793/16,441) were children under 15 years of age. Current thresholds for AKI were associated with mortalities greater than 5%. An admission creatinine greater than three times the age/weight predicted baseline value was associated with >5% mortality. An admission urea >10 mmol/L had approximately similar prognostic value. A urea >10 mmol/L was 3.5 times more common in adults than children. In children <15 years of age, urea was a better prognostic indicator of death than creatinine and, unlike creatinine, correlated with the plasma PfHRP2 concentration. The main limitations of this analysis are the lack of metadata documenting laboratory methods and wide heterogeneity in eligibility criteria, such as creatinine or urea admission values for inclusion.
Conclusions
Admission serum or plasma creatinine >3 times the age/weight predicted baseline value (KDIGO AKI stage 3) can be used to define severe malaria AKI. In children, urea is a better predictor of the true infection biomass and a better prognostic indicator for death. We recommend the following as defining criteria for severe malaria: either a urea (BUN) threshold of 10 mmol/L for both children and adults, or simple age-based thresholds representing approximately >3 times fold change in creatinine from predicted baseline. These updated thresholds identify between 4 and 8 times more children with severe malaria AKI who are at a high risk of death.
Author summary
Why was this study done?
- Acute kidney injury (AKI) has been thought to be rare in children and common in adults, based on the World Health Organization (WHO) definition which is a creatinine >265 μmol/L or a urea >20 mmol/L.
- However, these thresholds were based on data from adult patients. For creatinine, a threshold of 265 μmol/L represents a much greater decrease in glomerular filtration rate due to lower muscle mass (greater fold change from baseline) and so will underestimate the proportion of children with severe malaria AKI.
What did the researchers do and find?
- We pooled individual patient data from 14 prospective studies of severe malaria or severe paediatric disease, where urea or creatinine was measured on admission. This gave a total of more than 16,000 patients, the majority of whom were children.
- We then calibrated thresholds for urea and creatinine by determining values that resulted in more than 5% chance of death. The suggested updated thresholds are >3 times the age or weighted predicted baseline creatinine, or a urea >10 mmol/L.
- Under these revised thresholds, the number of children who would be classified as severe malaria AKI increases by 4- to 8-fold.
What do these findings mean?
- Current criteria substantially under-diagnose severe malaria AKI in children, even though the proportion with severe malaria AKI is lower in children than in adults.
- The WHO definition of severe malaria AKI should be updated. This will ensure children with severe malaria AKI are correctly identified and managed.
- Limitations of this study include lack of documentation of how laboratory measurements were taken, and substantial variation in which populations were eligible for inclusion in the individual studies.

Introduction
Severe malaria is a medical emergency requiring rapid assessment and immediate treatment with artesunate, preferably by the parenteral route [1]. Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria is characterised clinically by vital organ dysfunction usually as a direct consequence of a high parasite biomass and extensive parasitised erythrocyte sequestration. There is no absolute distinction between uncomplicated malaria and severe malaria, but rather a continuum of severity. The most appropriate definition of ‘severe malaria’ depends on the context. A more stringent definition is applied in a research setting compared to the inclusive indicators used in routine clinical care [1]. A general approach for defining severe malaria is to determine sets of clinical signs along with laboratory parameters which indicate an expected mortality greater than some threshold. For example, any clinical presentation with a diagnosis of malaria as the primary cause of illness and >5% chance of death could be categorised as ‘severe malaria’ [2]. That represents a mortality at least 50 times higher than that associated with ‘uncomplicated falciparum malaria’. This risk-based approach rationalises the definition, and allows it to be evidence-based.
Current definitions of severe malaria used by the World Health Organization (WHO) are based on expert consensus on the diagnostic and prognostic value of a range of clinical and laboratory parameters [1]. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is an important manifestation of severe falciparum malaria. It is a common presentation in adults in low transmission settings [3], and for these patients effective renal replacement therapy reduces mortality substantially [4]. Clinically significant AKI was thought to be less common in children with severe malaria in high-transmission settings, although it has long been recognised that elevated biochemical measures of reduced kidney function were associated with increased mortality [5,6]. The AKI thresholds now used as criteria to define severe malaria (a plasma or serum creatinine >265 μmol/L or blood urea nitrogen [BUN] >20 mmol/L) were based on observational studies done in adults. They were not modified for children, in whom muscle mass, and thus baseline plasma or serum creatinine levels, are lower. Recent studies from East Africa indicate that AKI in children hospitalised with malaria is more common than appreciated previously because the current thresholds for determining AKI, based on adult normal values, are too high for children [7,8]. Thus, the current creatinine threshold for severe malaria reflects a much greater reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in children, particularly the youngest children, than it does in adults. It is unclear what these high concentrations represent in terms of expected mortality in children presenting with suspected severe malaria.
We aimed to reevaluate and standardise the AKI thresholds to define severe malaria in adults and children by comparing the prognostic values of specific absolute and relative thresholds of serum creatinine and BUN using a pooled database comprising over 16,000 children and adults recruited into prospective studies of severe malaria. We compared the considered thresholds with the current thresholds for venous lactate concentration (one of the best measures of falciparum malaria disease severity which is independent of AKI [9,10]). The goal of the analysis was to determine optimal thresholds to be used in clinical management to identify both children and adults with suspected severe malaria who are at a substantially elevated risk of death, and characterise how general nephrology consensus criteria for AKI (e.g., KDIGO: https://www.kdigo.org) perform in severe malaria.
Methods
Ethics statement
This meta-analysis uses pseudonymised individual patient data with no identifying variables, so the ethics clearance was waived for the current analysis, as per the Oxford Tropical Research Ethics Committee guidance.
Data
Randomised trials and prospective observational cohort studies enrolling adults or children with suspected severe malaria with at least one baseline BUN (or urea) or creatinine measurement were eligible for inclusion. Studies of children or adults with severe febrile illness not specifically recruiting severe malaria but which had a subset of patients with severe malaria (e.g., the FEAST trial which recruited children with shock and febrile illness [11]) were also eligible for inclusion. Studies were identified from the WHO 2014 review of severe malaria [1], and a systematic review of the literature of all studies done since 2014 (see details of the systematic review in S1 Appendix). For all identified studies, study authors were contacted and asked to upload the data to the secure Infectious Diseases Data Observatory (IDDO) data platform. All data were then curated to a standardised CDISC SDTM format prior to analysis. Extensive data checking was carried out before pooling of data. A prospective protocol was not pre-registered before data analysis. A high-level analysis plan was drafted as part of the data request (S2 Appendix). The analyses were conducted according to PRISMA-IPD guidelines, apart from risk of bias assessments which were not relevant for this meta-analysis (S1 Checklist).
Analysis population
The primary analysis population consisted of patients in the pooled database who had all of the following recorded:
- A confirmed malaria infection at admission/enrolment (microscopy or rapid diagnostic test);
- Age either directly recorded or imputed from weight or height;
- Coma status at presentation;
- Mortality outcome at hospital discharge or by day 28 after admission;
- Admission plasma or serum creatinine or BUN measurement.
Outcomes and exposure definitions
The primary outcome was within-hospital mortality up to day 28. Many of the older studies did not systematically record the time to death, and so we use a binary outcome of died versus survived. The secondary outcome was the plasma Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein 2 (PfHRP2) concentration: this was chosen because it is a proxy measurement of the parasite biomass and thus the severity of the falciparum malaria infection [12,13].
Three exposure variables were defined: (i) the admission BUN; (ii) the admission creatinine; and the (iii) admission fold change in creatinine from the predicted baseline normal value. All analyses used log-transformed creatinine or BUN because the values are approximately log-normally distributed. The primary exposure-outcome analyses were performed on the complete-case datasets: all patients who had a measured BUN or creatinine, respectively. This is because missingness of BUN or creatinine measurements was almost entirely due to individual studies not taking these measurements (S1 Fig). We use molar BUN concentrations which are the same as molar urea concentrations (whereas in mg/dL the blood urea is 2.14 times the BUN concentration).
Statistical analysis
Regression modelling. All regression models included coma (yes/no; Glasgow Coma score <11 in adults, Blantyre Coma score <3 in children) as an independent predictor of outcome as this was recorded systematically across all studies and it is the strongest predictor of death. We did not include other clinical or laboratory variables as these were not consistently recorded, and we were primarily interested in the univariate relationship between the exposure (creatinine or BUN) and death. All regression models estimated age-dependent relationships between the exposure variables and death (interaction term between age as a continuous variable and the exposure variable), modelled using a tensor-product smooth between the exposure variable and age with cubic regression splines. We also explored models that categorised age divided into three categories: < 5, [5,15), and ≥15 years. Nested random intercepts were specified for each study and study site. All models included a temporal spline for calendar year as there have been substantial improvements in treatment and supportive care over the 40-year period over which these studies were conducted; hence, time could plausibly confound the relationship between exposure values and the outcome.
For the analysis comparing the prognostic value of BUN versus creatinine, we included only the subset of patients who had both values recorded at baseline. For the comparative analysis examining the relationship between plasma lactate and mortality, we included only patients in the primary analysis population who also had a recorded baseline hemoglobin or hematocrit measurement. An interaction term was included for hemoglobin above 5 g/dL. If hemoglobin was missing, but the hematocrit was recorded, the hemoglobin was imputed using a 1/3 transformation from hematocrit (%) to hemoglobin (g/dL), S2 Fig [14].
For the creatinine analysis, we compared the absolute creatinine values (μmol/L) and the creatinine fold change relative to a predicted age- and weight-adjusted normal baseline value. As pre-illness baseline creatinine was not available for any patients, it was estimated. To estimate the normal baseline values in children under 15 years, we compared two separate approaches: the Pottel equation which is based on age only (baseline Cr (0.244 / 120) [15]; and the Schwartz equation which is based on height only (15]. We then compared the predicted baseline creatinine values with the observed recovery values in a subset of patients recruited into the TRACT trial in Malawi who had follow-up creatinine and BUN both measured at 28, 90 and 180 days post-admission (n = 404 patients with ages ranging from 2 months to 12 years). This assumes the later measurements were equivalent to baseline values. The normal baseline values for patients over 15 years of age were estimated using the well-established Cockcroft–Gault equation, assuming a normal creatinine clearance of 120 mL/min. This equation was chosen as it incorporates both age and weight. The primary analysis used the age- and weight-based predicted baseline values (Pottel equation for children and Cockcroft-Gault equation for adults) because age was missing in only 6 patients and weight was missing in only 5% of patients. A sensitivity analysis explored compared the results when using the Schwartz equation (based on height) for the predicted baseline creatinine.
Single imputation of age, weight and height. To calculate creatinine fold change in all patients with measured creatinine values at baseline using age, weight or height, we performed single imputation using chained equations for age, weight, height, mid-upper arm circumference and the key laboratory parameters (lactate, creatinine, BUN, bicarbonate, hemoglobin). The single imputation included the mortality outcome, sex, study and study site. We used random forests for the multiple imputation model as it allows for non-linear relationships between variables (notably relationship between age, weight and height is non-linear). Visual checks of the imputed versus complete case bivariate distributions were carried out to check the imputation outputs (S3 Fig). Single imputation was used because age was missing in only 6 patients in the creatinine analysis dataset; and weight was only missing in 503 patients (5%) in the creatinine analysis dataset. Height was missing in 2,134 patients (22%). Standardised differences and Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) statistic were used to compare imputed with observed data, stratified by age (S3 Table).
Threshold estimation. In order to have comparable thresholds across different laboratory measurements, we estimated approximate values at which expected mortality was above 5%. This used the posterior predictive distribution of mortality outcomes from each Bayesian regression model, ignoring random effect terms (values set to zero). Thresholds were then chosen as values for which approximately 90% of the posterior mass was above 5% (function posterior_epred).
Changes to the planned analysis. Relative to the initial analysis plan, the primary exposure-outcome analyses were restricted to complete cases rather than imputed data, because missingness of creatinine and urea was almost entirely determined at the study level rather than at the patient level, so that imputation would have required imputing an entire study’s values (S1 Fig). In response to peer review, we added an analysis of random-effect variance components with median odds ratios (S1 Table; S18 and S19 Figs), quantitative imputation diagnostics (S3 Table) and receiver operating characteristic curves (S11 Fig); these are additional reporting of the planned analysis and did not change any estimates. The analyses of hyperkalaemia, acidosis and the relationship with plasma PfHRP2 were exploratory and data-driven, prompted by unexpected patterns in the pooled data.
Software. Bayesian generalised linear models with penalised spline terms were fitted for in-hospital mortality (Bernoulli likelihood, logit link) using the brms package which constructs the spline bases via mgcv and uses stan to estimate posterior distributions [16–18]. Each smooth term is decomposed into an unpenalised component (population-level coefficient), and one or more penalised components whose basis coefficients are given zero-mean Gaussian priors each with its own standard deviation
The primary analysis models used a tensor-product smooth (t2) between the exposure and age constructed from two marginal cubic regression spline bases of dimension five, giving 24 basis coefficients and three separate penalties (one for each marginal main effect and one for their interaction). The calendar-year smooth used a thin-plate regression spline basis of dimension 10. The supporting models in which age was divided into three categories used a univariate cubic regression spline basis of dimension 10 for the exposure, together with a factor-smooth interaction (bs = “fs", k = 10, m = 1) that penalises the deviation of each age group’s curve from the common curve. Basis dimensions set an upper bound on flexibility; the estimated curvature is determined by the posterior distribution of PfHRP2 outcome using lme4 (maximum likelihood estimation) [19].
We used the brms default priors, which were not modified. The prior on the standard deviation parameters (smoothing standard deviations of every spline term and the standard deviations of the nested study and study-site random intercepts) and the intercept were Student-t(3, 0, 2.5) (three degrees of freedom, location zero and scale 2.5, truncated at zero for standard deviation parameters). The remaining population-level coefficients (coma status and the unpenalised components of the smooths) were given improper flat priors. This shrinkage controlled model complexity; no additional variable selection or tuning of penalties was carried out. The number of observations was large relative to the number of basis coefficients. Between-study and between-site heterogeneity in mortality risk was summarised for all fitted models by the posterior standard deviations of the random effects and by the corresponding median odds ratios (S1 Table) [20], with the estimated study- and site-level random effects shown in S18 and S19 Figs. To compare the effects of creatinine and urea exposure effects against each other and against the across-study and site variance, a multivariable model was fitted with both exposures standardised (zero mean and unit variance).
All Bayesian models were fitted using four chains of 2,000 iterations, of which the first 1,000 were discarded as warmup. Convergence was satisfactory for all reported models (PfHRP2 outcome using lme4 (maximum likelihood estimation) [19]. Imputation using chained equations with random forests used the mice package [21]. Euler diagrams (generalisation of Venn diagrams to up to 5 categories) were estimated from imputed data (BUN, hemoglobin, lactate) using the R package eulerr [22]. Detailed model fits and parameter estimates are given in the accompanying github repository.
Results
Participants
Individual patient data from 14 studies were pooled, providing data from a total of 22,663 patients. After excluding one study with unreliable creatinine measurements and one study that had no urea or creatinine data, 16,441 patients from 12 studies had a recorded or imputed age, coma status, parasitological confirmation of malaria at baseline, a recorded mortality outcome, and at least one baseline measurement of creatinine or urea (BUN). These 16,441 patients were included in the analysis population (9,848 patients had creatinine measured on admission; 12,537 patients had urea (BUN) measured on admission; and 5,944 patients had both), S4 Fig. Table 1 shows the demographic characteristics of the patients in the analysis population stratified by study. The majority of patients were children (n = 13,793 <15 years, 84%) and from Africa (n = 13,533, 82%). 9.5% of all patients died within 28 days of admission (n = 1,569/16,441).
Age and weight dependent distribution of creatinine and urea in severe malaria patients
Fig 1 shows the relationship between weight (kg, square root scale) or age (years, square root scale) and the admission serum or plasma creatinine (left panels) and urea (right panels; both on the log10 scale). For both creatinine and urea there was, as expected, a clear relationship between weight/age and admission values, with substantial inter-individual variation. When comparing children (defined as patients younger than 15 years of age) versus adults (≥15 years), the median serum or plasma creatinine values were 45 µmol/L (interquartile range [IQR]: 31, 64) versus 155 µmol/L (IQR: 113, 256), respectively; i.e., they were approximately 3.4 times higher in adults. For urea the median values were 4.6 mmol/L (IQR: 2.9, 7.5) versus 10.9 mmol/L (IQR: 6.4, 21.4), i.e., approximately 2.4 times higher in adults. The larger difference between creatinine values in adults versus children likely reflects the stronger dependence of creatinine on muscle mass and hence weight/age. This was also reflected by a systematic difference in the creatinine/urea ratios between children and adults (Fig 2). The relationship between weight and urea was consistent across five large studies [11,26,28,30,31] which all used the portable i-STAT machine (Abbott) to measure BUN (S5 Fig).

Prognostic value of creatinine and BUN
To explore the relationships between creatinine, urea and mortality by day 28 we divided patients into four categories for renal biomarkers (creatinine: ≤65, (65, 130], (130, 265], >265 µmol/L; urea: ≤5, (5, 10], (10, 20], >20 mmol/L). As coma on admission has the greatest prognostic significance of all clinical variables, we estimated the proportion of patients who died in each creatinine and urea category, subdivided by coma status on admission (yes/no) and age (<15 years versus ≥15 years). Only 119 out of 6,553 children under 5 years of age with a measured creatinine had values above 265 μmol/L, nearly all of whom were from the TRACT study (83%) with corresponding low mortality by day 28. Apart from this group, in patients meeting the current WHO AKI threshold for defining severe malaria (plasma or serum creatinine >265 μmol/L or urea >20 mmol/L), the observed mortality was 5% or more in both children and adults, even without coma on admission (Fig 3). Mortality was greater than 5% for threshold values of 130 μmol/L for creatinine and 10 mmol/L for urea (i.e., half the current thresholds).

There was clear heterogeneity between the absolute plasma or serum creatinine value and mean case fatality ratio by age (Fig 3). The same absolute creatinine thresholds implied substantially different expected mortalities in children versus adults. This was less apparent for urea. In order to harmonise comparisons between adults and children, we estimated a creatinine fold change from predicted baseline values and used that as the primary exposure variable. Using 6-month follow-up data from children in Malawi recruited into the TRACT trial to provide normal paediatric baseline values, there was a clear linear relationship between age and baseline creatinine, the slope of which was well approximated by the Schwartz equation (it had a systematic upwards bias, but the residuals were less correlated with the baseline value relative to the Pottel equation, Figs 4 and S6). Height, age and weight all had approximately the same predictive value (explaining roughly 50% of the variance in baseline creatinine values in these data). As expected, urea did not vary by age or weight, apart from in the youngest children (<2 years), Fig 4. Very young children (under 1 year of age) had baseline urea concentration around 30% lower than the older children (approximately 2.0 mmol/L versus 2.85 mmol/L).

As expected, given the large variation in baseline creatinine by age, there was considerable variation in predicted mortality as a function of the absolute creatinine values by age (Figs 5 and S7). In patients without coma, the probability of >5% mortality exceeded 90% for a creatinine around 80 μmol/L in children, compared with around 200 μmol/L in adults. However, under the same model structure, there was very little residual heterogeneity by age in the predicted mortality relationship when using the creatinine fold change based on the Pottel equation for children and the Cockcroft-Gault equation for adults. There was also no clear age heterogeneity in children when using the Schwartz equation (S8 Fig). A three times increase in predicted baseline creatinine (i.e., KDIGO AKI stage 3) was associated with a mortality >5% in all age groups (Fig 5). This was lower for the Schwartz equation which predicted higher baseline values. For urea, there was considerably less heterogeneity between the absolute value and the predicted risk of death. Older children and adults had slightly higher threshold values (between 12 and 14 mmol/L) associated with >0.9 probability that death would occur in >5% of patients, Fig 5. There was no clear relationship with mortality outcomes (S16 Fig).

In a multivariable logistic regression model comparing creatinine fold change and urea (BUN) (both on the log2 scale), with an interaction by age category, adjusted for coma status, a doubling in admission urea was a better predictor of death than a doubling in admission creatinine fold change in all age groups under 15 years. In adults urea and creatinine had similar prognostic value (S9-S11 Figs). A doubling in plasma or serum creatinine relative to the age/weight predicted baseline was associated with an adjusted odds ratio for death of 1.91 (95% credible interval [CrI]: 1.39, 2.62) in patients >15 years, whereas for all age groups in children under 15 years the CrI included 1. In comparison, a doubling of urea was associated with an increased risk of death in all age groups with estimated odds ratio between 1.2 (95% CrI: 1.02, 1.81; >15 years) and 2.09 (95% CrI: 1.39, 3.17; children between 5 and 15 years). Overall, creatinine fold change, BUN and lactate had similar prognostic values for death by day 28 with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of approximately 0.72 (S11 Fig). However, this masked important heterogeneity between adults and children. In children, both the urea and creatinine thresholds had low sensitivity (50% or lower) but high specificity for death; in adults the sensitivity was much higher (82% for urea >10 mmol/L), but the specificity was only 50% (Table 2). In comparison, a lactate threshold of 5 mmol/L had similar sensitivities (∼65%) and specificities (∼75%) in all age groups. Residual heterogeneity in baseline mortality risk between studies and sites (nested random effects) was consistent across all model parameterisations (S1 Table) and approximately the same order of magnitude of effect as one standard deviation change in the log10 urea or the log2 creatinine fold change (S2 Table).
Hyperkalemia in severe malaria
Hyperkalemia is associated with both AKI and acidosis (of any cause). Clinically significant hyperkalemia (K+ > 6.5 mmol/L) on admission was recorded in 3.9% (583/14,952) of patients with admission potassium values. Nearly all were in children (only 19 out of 2,377 [0.8%] were in adults). Elevated creatinine or urea concentrations were only weakly predictive of hyperkalemia (Fig 6) with a large number of children with hyperkalemia and BUN <10 mmol/L. Very low bicarbonate (<10 mEq/L) was the strongest predictor of hyperkalemia.

Association of AKI with parasite biomass
In the pooled database, there were 4,116 patients from 4 studies with admission plasma PfHRP2 and creatinine both measured, and 7,697 patients from 5 studies with admission plasma PfHRP2 and BUN both measured. All were children under 15 years of age. Plasma PfHRP2 is the best quantitative marker of the total parasite biomass and thus the true underlying severity of the infection [12]. We assessed its relationship with admission creatinine fold change and urea. In the TRACT trial, there was a large subgroup of patients with very low plasma PfHRP2 and high creatinine and high BUN with an unexpectedly low case fatality ratio (S12 and S13 Figs). The reason for this was unclear. In patients with a plasma PfHRP2 > 1,000 ng/ml (i.e., patients likely to have true severe malaria [13]), there was little correlation between plasma PfHRP2 and creatinine fold change, but there was a strong correlation between plasma PfHRP2 and BUN (S14 Fig).
Attributable fraction of AKI in children and adults
We used the full analysis dataset with multiple imputation for missing data to estimate the proportion of patients with a presentation of reduced kidney function (urea >10 mmol/L), versus cerebral malaria, severe anaemia (hemoglobin <5 g/dL), and lactic acidosis (lactate ≥5 mmol/L). Seventy-five percent of patients in the analysis dataset (12,253/16,441) met one of these categories (10,134/13,793 children and 2,119/2,648 adults). Fig 7 shows the estimated individual proportions and overlaps for each category. A urea >10 mmol/L was a dominant manifestation in adults (54%), but only occurred in 16% of children (i.e., 3.5 times more common in adults). Very high urea concentrations (>30 mmol/L) occurred in approximately 3.5% of children and 15% of adults (i.e., 4 times more common in adults). Analysis of the complete case data gave very similar proportions.

Identifying patients with severe malaria is essential for appropriate triage, and also for the correct evaluation of therapies. The current definition of severe malaria used in clinical research comprises a list of clinical or laboratory abnormalities, any one of which fulfils the definition. All, except the anaemia criterion (hemoglobin less than 5 g/dL), are associated with a mortality >5% [2]. The European Commission has established a new EU Sanctions Office to improve sanctions implementation, strengthen enforcement and prevent circumvention across the bloc.
nnounced on 18 November 2026, the new office will bring together expertise covering the entire sanctions process, from policy development to implementation, enforcement and cooperation with third countries. The changes will take effect on 16 January 2027.
According to the Commission, the office will support EU Member States through faster compliance guidance, improved data sharing, and economic and technical analysis to ensure more consistent implementation of sanctions.
Its responsibilities will cover all EU sanctions regimes, particularly those concerning Russia, Belarus, Iran, North Korea and Syria, as well as measures related to hybrid threats and organized crime.
The initiative follows the expansion of EU sanctions in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Since the beginning of the war, the EU has adopted 21 sanctions packages, increasing the need for stronger coordination and enforcement.
As previously highlighted, the EU’s 21st sanctions package introduced additional compliance requirements for shipping, including restrictions targeting Russia’s energy revenues and sanctions-circumvention networks.
More recently, the EU expanded sanctions against Russia’s shadow fleet support network, building on measures covering vessels providing operational support to sanctioned tankers, including bunkering and ship-to-ship transfer services.
The office will operate within the Commission’s Secretariat-General under the political responsibility of Commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque. It will bring together expertise from several Commission departments, including those responsible for financial services, trade, taxation and customs, and anti-fraud activities.
Working closely with Member States and international partners, we will reinforce implementation, close loopholes and prevent circumvention. A stronger, more coordinated European approach will make our sanctions more effective and our external action more credible.
… said Maria Luís Albuquerque, Commissioner for Financial Services and the Savings and Investments Union.
A key responsibility will be supporting the EU Sanctions Envoy in preventing sanctions circumvention, particularly through alternative trade routes, financial channels and procurement networks. This work will involve cooperation with third countries to address potential loopholes.
The Commission has also appointed Lars Danielsson as the new International Special Envoy for the Implementation of EU Sanctions. He will assume the position on 6 February 2027, succeeding David O’Sullivan.
Commenting on the initiative, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen emphasized the importance of effective implementation and enforcement.
To be effective, they must be fully implemented, rigorously enforced and protected against circumvention
… she stated, referring to EU sanctions.
The new structure is intended to strengthen coordination between EU institutions, Member States and international partners, while supporting more consistent enforcement across existing sanctions regimes.

Beijing has tightened export controls on a range of components used to manufacture drones, including the jet-turbine engines used in Russia's jet-powered "Geran" series of drones, according to regulations by China's Commerce Ministry that took effect on Nov. 18.
Both Russia and Ukraine rely on China for a wide range of drone components, with Russia increasingly substituting Chinese components for parts previously imported from the West. 
Exporters must now seek licenses to export certain drone components, including jet and electric drone engines, radio transmitters, and speed controllers, the Chinese Commerce Ministry announced in October. 
The tightened export controls were welcomed by Ukraine's commissioner for sanctions, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, who nonetheless cautioned that many components used in Russian drones are still not subject to export controls.
"We thank China for its new export controls on drone items," Vlasiuk said in a statement on social media.
Vlasiuk pointed out that while the new controls cover jet-engines, UAV radio modules, heavy brushless motors, and speed controllers, they don't include anti-jamming antennas (found in Russian Geran-2 drones), navigation modules, HARXON antennas, gimbal cameras, or Chinese manufactured servos (found in Geran-4 drones).
China's updated regulations encompass "only part of what matters for Russian weapons, but it is a start," Vlasiuk said. "We have shared detailed information on these components and their Chinese manufacturers, and we count on rigorous control of these exports."
Russian jet-powered drones have been increasingly used in Russia's campaign of strikes against Ukrainian civilian energy and logistical infrastructure. 
Jet-powered drones are significantly more difficult to shoot down than Russia's older, piston-engined drones, outpacing the majority of Ukraine's drone interceptors. Moreover, Russia is rapidly scaling production of these deadlier types, according to the Ukrainian government.
Russia has the capacity to launch up to 6,500 jet-powered Shahed-type drones at Ukraine in November,  Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on Nov. 16 in an interview with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL). That number represents about a 12-fold increase from the 530 drones Russia fired in August.

China has tightened export restrictions on some drone components that Russia uses in its weapons, including engines, radio modules, and electric motors. The new controls took effect on 18 November, but leave several Chinese-made parts found in some Russian drones, including anti-jamming antennas and navigation systems, outside the restrictions, Ukraine's sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said.
Russia relies heavily on Chinese-made components to manufacture and upgrade its drones, missiles, and other weapons, despite Ukraine's repeated calls for tighter controls on exports that help sustain Russia's war effort. The new restrictions could limit access to some of these technologies, but significant gaps remain.
Ukraine compared the list of controlled items with Chinese components identified in Russian Shahed and Geran drones, missiles, and reconnaissance UAVs. Vlasiuk welcomed the measures but said they cover only part of the equipment Russia uses to produce its weapons.
The rules require export licenses for specified drone-related products and technologies. They do not impose a blanket ban on their export.
Which components are covered?
According to Vlasiuk, the new controls cover jet engines with a thrust of at least 400 newtons, as well as other UAV engines with power output exceeding 16 kilowatts. These include engines used in jet-powered Geran variants.
The restrictions also cover radio modules with output power of at least 30 dBm or capable of controlling more than 10 drones, along with high-power brushless electric motors and their speed controllers.
Trending Now
However, several components identified in Russian weapons are not covered by these measures. They include controlled reception pattern antennas (CRPAs) with Chinese-made circuit boards found in Geran-2 drones, navigation modules, HARXON antennas, gimbal-mounted cameras, and servos used in Geran-4 drones.
"These controls cover only part of what matters for Russian weapons, but this is a start," Vlasiuk wrote on 18 November. He said Ukraine had shared detailed information about the components and their Chinese manufacturers with its partners and expected strict enforcement of the new rules.
The new controls could make it harder for Russia to obtain some components directly from Chinese suppliers. Their impact will depend on how strictly Beijing enforces the licensing requirements and whether Russian buyers can continue sourcing the equipment through intermediaries or alternative suppliers.

NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) Nov. 18.
Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday.
“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.”
Scientists use light to measure the vast distances of space. Light travels at about 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) a second in a vacuum. A ray of sunlight passing Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, about four hours to reach Neptune, and another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1. For comparison, a light-year is 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).
Even though the team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, the spacecraft is sending what is called a carrier signal, which typically conveys that data to Earth. Mission engineers used the carrier signal and trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day milestone. They continue to analyze the issue impacting the science and engineering data.
Humanity’s only probes in interstellar space, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Managed by JPL, they were only the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn, and the first to return high-resolution imagery, transforming our understanding of these worlds and their moons. Voyager 2 went on to study the ethereal ice giants, Neptune and Uranus. Both spacecraft continue to measure changes in the Sun’s magnetic field across vast distances.
“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”
In addition to their suite of scientific instruments, the Voyager probes carry a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph compiling images and sounds from Earth, as a message to any advanced civilization that might one day find it.
“Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward,” said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. “Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.”
Milestones, challenges
Traveling about 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), Voyager 1 in 2012 became the first spacecraft to leave the heliosphere, the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the Sun that deflects cosmic radiation, and enter interstellar space. Voyager 2, taking a different trajectory, crossed the boundary in 2018.
“The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere,” said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. “One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.”
Creative engineering solutions have enabled the probes to conserve energy and overcome challenges related to aging hardware, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer on the spacecraft. Earlier this year, engineers successfully turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives — a move not without risk — to help the spacecraft make the most of its 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator. Essentially a nuclear battery, the generator converts heat from decaying plutonium into electricity.
With the plutonium supply continually depleting, both Voyager probes lose about 4 watts of power each year. The latest energy-saving effort is expected to provide enough power for both spacecraft to keep their current suite of science instruments operating until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer.
As with all NASA spacecraft that venture to and beyond the Moon, communication between Earth and the Voyager probes is managed by the agency’s Deep Space Network, large antennas located at three facilities around the world.
“We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. “Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity’s silent ambassador to the stars.”
